overview.title: Understanding your data and choosing a measure of success
overview.chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning
overview.subsection: 6.1.3 Understanding your data; 6.1.4 Choosing a measure of success
overview.main_topic: Exploratory checks before training (samples, histograms, maps, missing values, class balance, target leaking) and picking a success metric aligned with business goals
overview.central_idea: Don't treat your dataset as a black box. Inspect it to see what makes it predictive and to catch problems such as missing values, class imbalance and target leaking. Then define success with a metric that matches your high-level goals, because that metric will guide every technical choice in the project.
overview.importance: These are the last two steps of 'define the task' before model development. Target leaking and a badly chosen metric are two of the most common reasons a project looks successful on paper and fails in practice.
learning_objectives: List the six data-exploration checks the book recommends and what each one detects.
Define target leaking and explain the medical-records example.
Apply the test 'is every feature available in the same form in production?'.
Explain why the success metric must align with higher-level (business) goals.

Match metrics to problem types: accuracy and ROC AUC for balanced classification; precision/recall or confusion-matrix counts for imbalanced, ranking or multilabel problems; custom metrics when needed.
prerequisites: Classification vs. regression and class labels (chapter 4).
Accuracy as a metric from earlier examples.

summary:
**6.1.3 Understanding your data** opens with "It's bad practice to treat a dataset as a black box." Before training, explore and visualize the data to learn **what makes it predictive** (which informs feature engineering) and to **screen for issues**:

- **Images or text**: look at a few samples and their labels directly.
- **Numerical features**: plot **histograms** to see value ranges and frequencies.
- **Location data**: plot it on a **map** and look for patterns.
- **Missing values**: note them for data preparation (covered next, p.204).
- **Classification**: **count instances per class**. If the classes are imbalanced, you must account for it.
- **Target leaking**: features that give information about the target but *may not be available in production*. The example is a model predicting whether someone *will be treated for cancer* from medical records that include "This person has been diagnosed with cancer." The target leaks into the inputs. The test to apply: *is every feature available in the same form in production?*

**6.1.4 Choosing a measure of success** begins with "To control something, you need to be able to observe it." You must define success (accuracy, precision and recall, customer retention rate). That metric **guides all technical choices** and should **align with higher-level goals** such as the customer's business success.

Metric guidance:

- **Balanced classification** (every class equally likely): **accuracy** and **ROC AUC** (area under the curve of the receiver operating characteristic).
- **Class-imbalanced, ranking, or multilabel** problems: **precision and recall**, or a metric built from **true/false positives/negatives**.
- Defining a **custom metric** is not unusual.

To see the range of metrics used in practice, the authors suggest browsing **Kaggle** competitions.

paragraphs.excerpt: It’s bad practice to treat a dataset as a black box. Before you start
paragraphs.what_it_says: Don't treat a dataset as a black box. Before training, explore and visualize it to learn what makes it predictive, which informs feature engineering, and to screen for potential issues.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Exploration does two jobs: it finds signal (what features matter) and it finds problems (noise, leaks, imbalance). Both are cheaper to handle before modeling than after.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It links to p.200, where not understanding how experts annotate forces you to treat the dataset as a black box. Here the book asks you to open the box as far as you can.

terminology.meaning: Beyond the book: the standard name for inspecting and visualizing data before modeling.
Designing input representations that make the target easier to learn.

connections: p.200: the black-box dataset and its limits on manual feature engineering.

paragraphs.excerpt: If your data includes images or natural language text, take a look at
paragraphs.what_it_says: For image or text data, look directly at a few samples and their labels.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Looking at raw examples quickly shows label errors, odd formats, duplicates and mismatches with production. The dish-photo failure on p.200 was caught by 'a quick look at user-uploaded data.'
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the cheapest sanity check there is.
connections: p.183: 'visualize your inputs to check for anomalies, and proofread your labels.'

paragraphs.excerpt: If your data contains numerical features, it’s a good idea to plot the
paragraphs.what_it_says: For numerical features, plot histograms to see the range and frequency of values.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Histograms show scale differences that call for normalization (p.152 house prices), skew, outliers, and placeholder values such as 0 or -999 that may stand for missing data.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Feature ranges directly affect preprocessing choices in 6.2.1.

terminology.meaning: A plot of how many values fall into each value range (bin).

connections: p.152: normalizing features and scaling targets in the house price example.

paragraphs.excerpt: If your data includes location information, plot it on a map. Do any
paragraphs.what_it_says: Plot location data on a map and check whether clear patterns emerge.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Spatial structure such as clusters, coverage gaps or regional label differences is easy to see on a map and hard to see in a table. It can also reveal sampling bias, for example data only from a few cities.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is relevant to projects like the satellite archaeology example.
connections: p.199: the satellite archaeology project's database of sites.

paragraphs.excerpt: Are some samples missing values for some features? If so, you’ll need to
paragraphs.what_it_says: Check whether some samples are missing feature values. If so, you will handle them during data preparation (next section).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Detecting missing values belongs to understanding the data. Fixing them belongs to preparing the data.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Missing values can silently break training or bias the model if they are left unhandled.

terminology.meaning: Feature entries with no recorded value for some samples.

connections: p.204: 'Handling missing values', for example the house-age feature in the house price data.

paragraphs.excerpt: If your task is a classification problem, print the number of instances of
paragraphs.what_it_says: For classification, count instances per class. If the classes are not roughly balanced, account for the imbalance.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Class balance affects which metrics make sense (6.1.4, a few lines later) and the baseline you must beat (p.205). With 99% of one class, predicting that class always gives 99% accuracy.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It connects directly to the metric choice on this page: imbalance means accuracy is not the right metric.

terminology.meaning: Some classes appear much more often than others.

connections: p.205: beating a baseline (the trivial majority-class predictor).

paragraphs.excerpt: Check for target leaking—the presence of features in your data that provide information
paragraphs.what_it_says: Check for target leaking, meaning features that give information about the targets but may not be available in production. In the example, a model predicts future cancer treatment from medical records that include 'This person has been diagnosed with cancer', so the target leaks into the data. Always ask whether every feature will be available in the same form in production.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A leaked feature lets the model 'cheat'. It is nearly a copy of the label, so validation scores look excellent, but at prediction time (before diagnosis) the feature does not exist yet and the model fails.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Leaks produce some of the most misleading results in ML, and the validation set will not reveal them because the leak is present there as well.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: leakage is often temporal. A feature recorded after the moment the prediction would be made is unavailable in production. Leakage can also come from preprocessing statistics computed on the test data, which the book warns against on p.152.

terminology.meaning: Input features that carry information about the target which won't be available, in the same form, when the model is used in production.

connections: p.152: never use quantities computed on test data, even for normalization.

paragraphs.excerpt: To control something, you need to be able to observe it. To achieve
paragraphs.what_it_says: To control something you have to observe it, and to succeed you must first define success: accuracy, precision and recall, or customer retention rate. The metric guides every technical choice and should directly align with higher-level goals such as the customer's business success.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The metric is the target you optimize toward when choosing architectures, hyperparameters and models. If it is misaligned with business value, you can improve the metric while the business outcome does not improve.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It determines the validation monitoring in 6.2 and how you report results to stakeholders (6.3.1).

terminology.meaning: A quantity that defines and measures how well the project meets its goal.
A business-level metric: the fraction of customers who keep using the product.

connections: p.208: explaining your work to stakeholders and setting expectations.

paragraphs.excerpt: For balanced classification problems, where every class is equally likely, accuracy and area
paragraphs.what_it_says: For balanced classification, accuracy and ROC AUC are common. For class-imbalanced, ranking or multilabel problems, use precision and recall or a metric that counts true/false positives/negatives. Custom metrics are not uncommon. Kaggle competitions show a wide range of problems and metrics.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Accuracy only treats all errors fairly when classes are balanced. Under imbalance it rewards ignoring the rare class. Precision and recall focus on the class you care about. ROC AUC measures how well a classifier ranks positives above negatives across all thresholds.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It gives a practical mapping from problem type to metric, which you can apply to the chapter's projects (fraud is imbalanced, and photo search is multilabel).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the ROC curve plots true positive rate against false positive rate as the decision threshold varies. AUC = 1 is a perfect ranking and AUC = 0.5 is random.

terminology.meaning: Receiver operating characteristic: TPR vs. FPR across thresholds.
Area under the ROC curve; threshold-independent ranking quality.
Fraction of predicted positives that are correct / fraction of actual positives that are found.

connections: p.197: fraud detection (imbalanced binary) and photo search (multilabel) framings.

concepts.name: Target leaking
concepts.definition: Features in the training data that provide information about the targets but may not be available in production.
concepts.intuition: The answer key is accidentally printed on the exam.
concepts.technical: The model learns a shortcut through the leaked feature; validation metrics are inflated because the leak is present there too.
concepts.significance: Produces models that look excellent offline and fail in deployment.
concepts.example: Predicting future cancer treatment with a 'diagnosed with cancer' feature.
concepts.misconception: A suspiciously high validation score is good news; it can indicate a leak.

concepts.name: Class imbalance
concepts.definition: Classes in a classification dataset are not roughly equally represented.
concepts.intuition: If 99% are 'no fraud', always saying 'no fraud' is 99% accurate and useless.
concepts.technical: Affects metric choice (precision/recall instead of accuracy) and may require reweighting or resampling.
concepts.significance: The book asks you to count instances per class and to account for imbalance.
concepts.misconception: High accuracy means a good classifier on imbalanced data.

concepts.name: Measure of success
concepts.definition: The metric that defines project success; it guides all technical choices and should align with higher-level goals.
concepts.intuition: You can only steer toward what you can observe.
concepts.technical: Used for validation monitoring, model selection and hyperparameter tuning.
concepts.significance: A misaligned metric means optimizing the wrong thing.
concepts.example: Accuracy, precision and recall, customer retention rate, custom metrics.
concepts.misconception: The loss function and the success metric are always the same; often they are not.

concepts.name: ROC AUC
concepts.definition: Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; the book lists it as common for balanced classification.
concepts.intuition: The probability that a random positive gets a higher score than a random negative.
concepts.technical: Beyond the book: the ROC curve plots TPR = TP/(TP+FN) against FPR = FP/(FP+TN) over all thresholds; AUC integrates it. 0.5 is random and 1.0 is perfect.
concepts.significance: Threshold-independent, so useful before you choose an operating point.
concepts.example: Comparing two binary classifiers' ranking quality.
concepts.misconception: AUC tells you the accuracy at your chosen threshold; it doesn't.

concepts.name: Precision and recall
concepts.definition: Metrics computed from true/false positives/negatives; recommended for imbalanced, ranking and multilabel problems.
concepts.intuition: Precision: when I say yes, am I right? Recall: of all the yeses, how many did I find?
concepts.technical: Beyond the book: precision = TP/(TP+FP), recall = TP/(TP+FN).
concepts.significance: Unlike accuracy, they are not dominated by the majority class.
concepts.example: Fraud detection: recall is the fraction of fraud caught, precision is the fraction of flags that are real fraud.
concepts.misconception: You can maximize both freely; raising the threshold usually trades recall for precision.

math.title: Accuracy, precision and recall from confusion-matrix counts
math.source_text: Not printed in the book; the page names 'precision and recall' and 'a metric that counts false positives, true positives, false negatives, and true negatives.'

variables.meaning: True positives: actual positives predicted positive.
True negatives: actual negatives predicted negative.
False positives: actual negatives predicted positive.
False negatives: actual positives predicted negative.

math.operations: Ratios of counts from the 2x2 confusion matrix.
math.purpose: Shows why the book recommends precision/recall over accuracy for imbalanced problems.
math.interpretation: Accuracy pools both classes, so the majority class dominates. Precision and recall look only at the positive class.
math.intuition: Accuracy asks how often you are right overall. Precision and recall ask how good you are at the rare thing you care about.
math.numerical_example: 1,000 transactions, 10 fraudulent. A model that always predicts 'legit': TP=0, FN=10, FP=0, TN=990. Accuracy = 990/1000 = **99%**, recall = 0/10 = **0%**, and precision is undefined (no positive predictions). A model that flags 20, of which 8 are fraud: TP=8, FP=12, FN=2, TN=978. Accuracy = 98.6%, precision = 8/20 = **40%**, recall = 8/10 = **80%**. The second model is far more useful despite lower accuracy.

deeper.title: Spotting target leaks in practice
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, practical heuristics that build on the book's question *is every feature available in the same form in production?*:
1. For each feature, write down **when** it is recorded relative to the moment the prediction is made.
2. Drop anything recorded after that moment (e.g., the diagnosis, in the book's example).
3. Be suspicious of near-perfect validation scores, especially on a hard problem.
4. Train a quick model and look at feature importance. A single feature that dominates is often a leak.
5. Check identifiers and file paths, which can encode the label (e.g., images sorted into class folders whose names appear in metadata).

deeper.title: Applying the metric guidance to the chapter's projects
deeper.body:
Inference, combining p.197's framings with this page's guidance:
- **Fraud detection** (binary, highly imbalanced): precision and recall rather than accuracy.
- **Photo search** (multilabel): precision and recall per tag or averaged.
- **Spam/offensive/acceptable** (three-way, probably imbalanced): per-class precision and recall.
- **Click-through rate** (scalar regression): a regression metric. The page's list is about classification.
- **Music recommendation**: ranking, so a ranking metric, plus a business metric such as engagement (p.212 mentions monitoring engagement).

misconceptions.claim: You can skip looking at your data if the model trains well.
misconceptions.correction: The book calls treating a dataset as a black box bad practice; exploration reveals predictive structure and issues like leaks and imbalance.

misconceptions.claim: A feature that strongly predicts the target is always a good feature.
misconceptions.correction: Not if it won't be available in the same form in production; that's target leaking (e.g., a 'diagnosed with cancer' feature).

misconceptions.claim: Accuracy is a fine metric for any classification problem.
misconceptions.correction: The book recommends accuracy/ROC AUC for balanced problems, and precision and recall (or TP/FP/FN/TN-based metrics) for imbalanced, ranking or multilabel problems.

misconceptions.claim: The success metric is a technical detail separate from business goals.
misconceptions.correction: The book says it should directly align with higher-level goals such as the customer's business success.

Never use quantities computed on test data (a form of leakage).

takeaways: Explore and visualize data before training: samples, histograms, maps, missing values, class counts.
Target leaking: a feature that reveals the target but won't be available in production; always ask whether each feature exists in the same form at prediction time.
Define success before building: the metric guides every technical choice and must align with business goals.
Balanced classification: accuracy, ROC AUC. Imbalanced, ranking or multilabel: precision and recall or TP/FP/FN/TN-based metrics.
Custom metrics are common; Kaggle competitions showcase the variety.

questions.question: Define target leaking in the book's words and give its example.
questions.answer: The presence of features in your data that provide information about the targets that may not be available in production. Example: predicting future cancer treatment from medical records that include 'This person has been diagnosed with cancer.'
questions.explanation: This is the last bullet of 6.1.3.

questions.question: For which kind of problem does the book list accuracy and ROC AUC as common metrics?
options: Balanced classification where every class is equally likely
questions.answer: Balanced classification where every class is equally likely
questions.explanation: For imbalanced, ranking and multilabel problems the book recommends precision and recall or TP/FP/FN/TN-based metrics instead.

questions.question: A fraud dataset has 1,000 transactions, 10 of them fraudulent. A model flags 20 transactions, 8 of which are fraud. Compute accuracy, precision and recall.
questions.explanation: This is the imbalanced setting the book mentions. A model that never flags anything would score 99% accuracy with 0% recall, which is why precision and recall are preferred here.

questions.question: Why does the book insist the success metric align with higher-level goals like the customer's business success?
questions.answer: Because the metric guides all technical choices in the project. If it is misaligned, you will optimize the wrong thing and may improve the metric without delivering value.
questions.explanation: 'Your metric for success will guide all of the technical choices you will make throughout the project.'

questions.question: Which exploration step does the book recommend for numerical features?
options: Plot a histogram of feature values
Look at a few samples and their labels
Print the number of instances per class
questions.answer: Plot a histogram of feature values
questions.explanation: Histograms show range and frequency. Maps are for location data, viewing samples is for images and text, and class counts are for classification targets.

questions.question: Why might a validation set fail to reveal target leaking?
questions.answer: The leaked feature is present in validation data too, so the model's shortcut works there and the scores look excellent. The problem only appears in production, where the feature is unavailable.
questions.explanation: Inference from the book's definition, which centers on availability in production.

questions.question: For a classification dataset you know, run through the book's six checks. Which one would you expect to reveal a problem, and what metric would you choose?
questions.explanation: Applying the checklist and the metric guidance from this page.
